opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing, but there is something genuinely new here. For the last several years, the story of progress in language models has been about scaling up training: more data, more parameters, more compute up front. And there's been growing evidence that this approach is hitting diminishing returns, partly because we're running low on high-quality training data, and partly because each additional order of magnitude of compute buys less noticeable improvement.

What o1 does differently is shift some of that effort to inference time. Instead of producing an answer in a single pass, the model generates a long chain of reasoning, explores different approaches, backtracks when something isn't working, and only then commits to an answer. And it's been trained, apparently with reinforcement learning, to do that reasoning well, rather than just being prompted to "think step by step." So you have a new axis along which to scale: let the model think longer and it tends to do better, at least on certain kinds of problems.

That's a real conceptual shift, and I think it's the most interesting thing to happen in this space in a while.

But I want to be careful. The improvements are concentrated in domains like math, coding, and certain science problems, where there's a clear right answer and you can verify it. That's exactly where reinforcement learning works well, because you have a clean reward signal. It's much less clear that this transfers to messier, open-ended tasks, the kinds of things that make up most real-world work, where there's no crisp notion of correctness.

And there's the usual caveat about benchmarks. A lot of the excitement is based on performance on things like competition math or coding contests. Those are impressive, but they're not the same as being useful in practice. We've seen over and over that benchmark gains don't translate cleanly into real-world utility, and there are persistent concerns about contamination and about what these tests actually measure.

So my view is: new, yes. A meaningful technical direction, yes. But it's not evidence that we're on some smooth exponential to general intelligence. It's one more tool, with its own strengths and limitations, and the hard work of figuring out where it actually helps people is still ahead of us.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd actually push back a little on the framing, because I'm not sure it represents something entirely new so much as a shift in where the scaling is happening. For the last several years, the story of progress in AI has been about scaling training: more data, more parameters, more compute at training time. And there's been a lot of debate about whether that's running out of steam, whether we've picked the low-hanging fruit, whether the data is running out.

What o1 does is take an idea that's been around in the research community for a while, which is that you can also scale inference-time compute. Instead of generating the answer in one shot, the model is allowed to generate a long chain of reasoning, explore different approaches, backtrack, check its own work, and spend much more compute per query. And OpenAI has trained the model, apparently with reinforcement learning, to do that kind of reasoning well rather than just prompting it to "think step by step."

So the reason I think it's significant is less about any single capability and more about what it says about the trajectory. If inference-time scaling is a real, reliable axis, then we have a second lever to pull, and that changes the economics and the development path for these systems. It also shifts what matters for applications. The cost of a query is no longer fixed; you can trade off latency and cost for accuracy, which is a very different way of thinking about deploying a model.

That said, I'd caution against overinterpreting the benchmark results. The gains are concentrated in domains like math, coding, and certain kinds of scientific problem solving, where there's a fairly clear notion of a correct answer and you can verify it. It's much less clear that this kind of reasoning transfers to open-ended tasks, or to the messy real-world problems where most of the value of AI actually lies. And there are a lot of unanswered questions about reliability. A model that reasons for longer can still reason confidently to the wrong conclusion, and because the chain of thought is hidden, it's harder for users to understand why.

So I'd say it's an important step, a genuinely new direction for the industry's investment, but the honest answer is that we don't yet know how far it goes.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s new is the way it uses computation at inference time—the time when the model is actually answering your question. Traditionally, the main way to make language models more capable has been to spend more compute on training. Here, there’s another dimension: can you get better answers by letting the model spend more computation working through a problem before it responds?

It’s not simply that the model produces a longer explanation. We’ve had chain-of-thought prompting for a while. The interesting idea is to train the model to use that intermediate work effectively—to try an approach, recognize when it isn’t working, and take a different path.

That’s particularly promising for problems where there’s a correct answer you can check, like math or coding. But I’d separate that from the broader claim that we’ve solved reasoning. Getting better at those tasks doesn’t automatically mean the model becomes more reliable in every setting. What’s new is a way to improve capabilities by spending more compute on a particular question, and the important question is how broadly that improvement carries over.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s new is the way it uses computation at inference time. We’ve gotten used to improving models by making them bigger and spending more on training. With o1, there’s another dimension: you can give the model more time to work through a problem before it produces an answer.

Now, asking a model to reason step by step isn’t new. The interesting part is training it to make that process more useful—to try an approach, recognize when it isn’t working, and try something else. That can make a substantial difference on problems where there’s a checkable answer, like math or coding.

But I’d separate that technical advance from the broader claim that we’ve solved reasoning. Doing better on those tasks doesn’t automatically mean the model will be more reliable in every setting. What’s exciting is that we have another way to improve performance. The question is where that extra computation actually buys us something, and at what cost.
